stories.title: Welltower Reports Revenue and Income Growth From Senior Housing Investments
stories.excerpt: Welltower, an investment firm focused on senior and assisted living communities, reported continued balance sheet improvement in the second quarter of 2026. The real estate investment trust (REIT) announced a slew of acquisitions, such as the Amica Senior Lifestyles portfolio consisting of 38 communities for $1.91 billion, as well as the disposition of $7.2 billion in outpatient medical properties, Welltower announced in a Tuesday earnings call. On July 2, Welltower also closed on a deal to acquire five properties currently under development in Canada for about $459 million with completion dates in 2027. Overall, the Ohio-based firm invested $9.5 billion in the U.S., Canada and the U.K. since the beginning of the year, Shankh Mitra, CEO of Welltower, said during the earnings call. “As the Welltower business system continues to mature, our ability to increase cash flow following an acquisition has become both more significant and more repeatable,” Mitra said. “That distinction matters. Spread investing and cost of capital arbitrage are not value creation, nor are they durable investment strategies. Our focus is different. We seek to acquire assets at a fair price, based on a reasonable view of their prospective cash flows while retaining for our owners the upside we believe our platform can create beyond that.” Funds from operations (FFO) in the second quarter reached $1.60 per share compared to $1.28 per share from the same period last year, while revenue for the quarter was $3.54 billion, an increase from the $2.55 billion recorded on a year-over-year basis. Net income was $12.2 billion, compared to $10.6 billion in the second quarter of 2025. Welltower also saw a 5.2 percent growth in revenue per occupied room, with the average number of occupied rooms in its portfolio at 100,410 compared to 96,800 on a year-over-year basis. bullets: Welltower acquired Amica Senior Lifestyles: 38 communities, $1.91B in Q2 2026.
Senior housing REIT deployed $9.5B across U.S., Canada, U.K. year-to-date.
Welltower divested $7.2B in outpatient medical properties; rebalancing toward senior housing.
stories.summary: Welltower, a senior and assisted living-focused REIT, reported strong Q2 2026 results, announcing the $1.91B acquisition of 38 Amica Senior Lifestyles communities and $459M in five Canadian development deals closing in 2027. The firm deployed $9.5B overall across North America and the U.K. year-to-date while divesting $7.2B in outpatient medical properties. CEO Shankh Mitra highlighted the firm's maturing ability to increase cash flow post-acquisition and leverage cost-of-capital arbitrage.
stories.impact: Welltower's aggressive capital deployment into senior housing—$1.91B in a single portfolio buy—signals sustained institutional conviction in aging-demographic tailwinds and pricing power in that asset class. The $7.2B medical divestment reflects capital rotation away from healthcare office, which has structural headwinds; this redeployment into senior living underscores where institutional capital sees better risk-adjusted returns, potentially crowding multifamily developers out of senior-focused development in core markets (Sun Belt, Florida, Southwest).

stories.title: Podcast: The Check Engine Light for CRE, with FTL President Clayton Callander
stories.excerpt: Clayton Callander is the founder of FTL (Field Technologies), a diagnostic platform built to give commercial buildings something like a check-engine light, closing the service gap for the roughly 95% of properties that enterprise vendors like Honeywell and Siemens can’t economically reach. Before founding FTL, Clayton spent seven years maintaining nuclear systems aboard a US Navy submarine, worked at SpaceX, and earned his MBA from Harvard Business School. He built FTL for the people fixing America’s commercial buildings because he used to be one of them, and the tool he needed didn’t exist yet. Clayton is based in San Francisco, CA. (00:00) – Intro: Why Six Million Commercial Buildings Have No Real-Time Data (01:10) – Meet Clayton Callander, Founder of Field Technologies (02:40) – The Telephone Game: What Happens When an HVAC Unit Breaks (05:50) – Zach’s Take: Preventative Maintenance’s 20-Year Elusive Goal (07:10) – It’s an Access Problem, Not a Technology Problem (09:40) – Why Building Controls Stay Complicated and Expensive (13:10) – What FTL Does (16:50) – Pricing FTL at a Fraction of Traditional Controls (20:20) – Why It’s Called Facilities Triage (22:20) – Which Asset Classes Are Ready for FTL (25:00) – What 60 Site Deployments Taught FTL (26:30) – Unlocking the Other Six Million Buildings (29:30) – LoRaWAN Explained: Why Not Wi-Fi (32:30) – Proprietary vs. Open Systems: A VC’s View (36:00) – Collaboration Superpower: Immanuel Kant (Wikipedia) and Ding Huan (Wikipedia) Learn more: –Visit FTL –Clayton Callander on LinkedIn NYC Real Estate Week: -CTO Exchange & Hackathon: 3-in-1 event on Oct. 19 featuring C-suite roundtables, a hackathon and the Power AI & Tech Awards reception (invite-only). Email ecohen@commercialobserver.com for info. CRE Events coming up: –Institutional Investors & PE Forum:
bullets: FTL (Field Technologies) diagnostic platform targets 95% of commercial buildings without enterprise vendor coverage.
Clayton Callander founded FTL to solve preventative maintenance gaps via real-time building diagnostics.
FTL prices at fraction of traditional building controls; focuses on HVAC and systems monitoring.
stories.summary: Field Technologies (FTL), founded by Clayton Callander, is a diagnostic platform offering check-engine-light functionality for commercial real estate—targeting the roughly 6 million buildings that enterprise vendors like Honeywell and Siemens cannot economically serve. The platform runs preventative maintenance, HVAC diagnostics, and building-systems monitoring at a fraction of traditional controls pricing, addressing a structural service gap in the industry.
stories.impact: For multifamily developers and operators, FTL's low-cost diagnostic platform could reduce capital and operational expenditure on building systems and emergency repairs post-delivery. If widely adopted, it lowers cost of ownership, improves asset yields, and extends equipment life—potentially improving pro forma returns on new builds and repositioning projects across all markets. However, this is a facilities-tech story with indirect bearing on development feasibility or demand; impact is operational margin, not market timing or capital availability.

stories.title: 60 Guilders, Sentry Realty Snap Up 1441 Broadway for $240M
stories.excerpt: The neon lights continue to shine bright on Broadway for 60 Guilders and Sentry Realty. The partnership just snapped up 1441 Broadway, a 550,000-square-foot office tower in Midtown Manhattan, for approximately $240 million, Commercial Observer has learned. The estate of LH Charney was the seller. Newmark’s Adam Spies and Adam Doneger arranged the sale. 60 Guilders CEO Kevin Chisholm led the deal in-house along with Jordana Rosenzweig, vice president of acquisitions at the firm. Sentry Realty’s Alen Mamrout and Joe Mamrout led the deal along with Yossi Althkefati. The deal marks the third purchase in the vicinity for the buyer group, which bought 1375 Broadway in December 2024 from Savanna — refinancing it with a $213 million loan earlier this year — and bought the 250,000-square-foot building at 1370 Broadway in January 2025 for $76 million. Newmark’s Jordan Roeschlaub, Nick Scribani and Ricky Braha arranged a roughly 70 percent loan-to-cost floating-rate acquisition loan from Fortress for the 1441 Broadway purchase, sources said. Situated between West 40th and West 41st streets, close to both Bryant Park and Times Square, the 33-story Art Deco building — also known as 10 Times Square — was erected in 1930. The building’s occupancy sits around 90 percent today with below-market leases, and the buyer group plans to improve the building, its tenancy and its cash flow over time, sources said. Still, 1441 Broadway has had plenty of leasing momentum of late. In March, Juicy Couture’s distribution company NYC Alliance signed an 11-year, 50,000-square-foot lease at the property, moving its headquarters from 1411 Broadway. Last April, four tenants took space at the building, including clothing rental service Style Theory, which signed a 14,634-square-foot lease; the Pekoe Group, which took the entire 25th floor encompassing 12,982 square feet; Mint Medical, which leased 3,736 square feet on the 24th floor; and factory services firm KDI, which signed a deal for 2,752 square
bullets: 60 Guilders, Sentry Realty acquire 1441 Broadway, Midtown Manhattan office, $240M.
Buyers already own 1375 Broadway ($213M refi, Dec 2024) and 1370 Broadway ($76M, Jan 2025).
Fortress provides ~70% LTC floating-rate acquisition loan; three Broadway deals in 18 months.
stories.summary: 60 Guilders and Sentry Realty purchased 1441 Broadway, a 550,000-sq-ft office tower in Midtown Manhattan, for approximately $240M from the LH Charney estate. The partnership financed the deal with a ~70% LTC floating-rate acquisition loan from Fortress. This marks their third Broadway-corridor acquisition in 18 months (1375 Broadway, Dec 2024; 1370 Broadway, Jan 2025), signaling aggressive office positioning in the heart of Manhattan.
stories.impact: Heavy office acquisition and refi activity on Broadway signals investor appetite for selective Midtown office repositioning, likely office-to-residential conversion plays given the 2024–2025 timing and trophy-asset profile. Fortress's willingness to lend 70% LTC on speculative office indicates moderate capital thaw for ground-floor commercial real estate. This does NOT directly affect multifamily development demand or supply in NYC but may compete for conversion capital and construction financing in Midtown; monitor whether these office conversions pull contractors and subcontractors away from pure multifamily new supply in outer boroughs and suburbs.

stories.title: 222 Broadway Conversion’s Stop-Work Order Not Tied to ‘Safety Issues’: Developer
stories.excerpt: New York City’s office-to-residential conversion wave hit another snag less than a month after columns buckled during an apartment transformation project at the former Pfizer headquarters in Midtown. Construction was halted last week by New York City’s Department of Buildings (DOB) at 222 Broadway in the Financial District, where GFP Real Estate is converting the former 31-story office building into a 788-unit luxury apartment tower. The Wall Street Journal first reported the stop-work order, which was issued after city inspectors determined the project’s contractor, Leeding Builders Group, and engineering firm, DeSimone Consulting Engineers, did not immediately disclose cracks formed on the Lower Manhattan building’s newly added 32nd floor. A GFP spokesman said the top-floor cracks were discovered in March and quickly repaired. The building is stable, with the project’s shutdown stemming from when the damage should have been reported and is not tied to “safety issues,” the spokesman said. The developer said leasing is underway and it expects to complete the project within a year. “Our structural engineers immediately identified and addressed this issue in March upon inspection and we subsequently had the proposed repairs reviewed by a third-party structural inspector to ensure that it was safely completed,” the GFP spokesman said. “At no point during construction has the building’s stability been compromised.’ The 222 Broadway project is among a series of office-to-resi projects throughout New York City totaling more than 16,000 units. Despite the headlines resulting from MetroLoft and David Werner Real Estate Investment’s Pfizer building conversion, the nation’s largest office-to-resi project, capital investments in these projects is not expected to slow, Commercial Observer reported last week. Leeding Builders Group, DeSimone Consulting Engineers and DOB didn’t immediately return requests for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobse
bullets: GFP Real Estate's 222 Broadway office-to-residential conversion (788 units) hit DOB stop-work order.
Contractor Leeding Builders Group failed to immediately disclose floor cracks discovered in March; non-safety issue.
Comes one month after Pfizer HQ conversion suffered structural column buckling; conversion velocity slowing.
stories.summary: GFP Real Estate's conversion of 222 Broadway (a 31-story Financial District office building into 788-unit luxury apartments) was halted by NYC's Department of Buildings after the contractor and engineer failed to immediately disclose cracks on a newly added 32nd floor. The developer denied safety concerns and said leasing is underway, but the stop-work order highlights regulatory scrutiny. The project is one of many NYC office-to-residential conversions and follows a column-buckling incident at the Pfizer conversion in Midtown last month.
stories.impact: NYC office-to-residential conversions are hitting execution headwinds (regulatory scrutiny, structural surprises, contractor compliance gaps) that may delay delivery timelines and inflate capex on projects in flight. This increases cost of capital and extends entitlement/construction risk for conversion deals, potentially pricing out smaller sponsors and consolidating conversion volume into large-cap developers with compliance infrastructure. For multifamily developers considering conversion vs. ground-up in NYC, the regulatory friction and construction unknowns now favor new supply in outer boroughs and suburbs where approval and execution are more predictable, shifting competitive advantage away from Manhattan conversions in 2026–2027.

stories.title: Agentic AI Startup Uniti Draws More Clients Amid $12M Series A
stories.excerpt: Uniti, an agentic artificial intelligence platform for real estate property managers, is experiencing rapid growth in client demand and funding as proptech companies compete to solve large operators’ everyday workflow challenges. Founded in February 2024, the Manhattan-based startup has seen demand for its agentic AI services grow across real estate asset classes, including with customers such as Regus, StorQuest, RHP Properties, Storage King USA and others. The company’s agentic AI layer can run leasing, maintenance, collections, reviews and renewals across voice, email, SMS and chat for operators in self-storage, manufactured housing, multifamily, senior living and flexible workspace. The company is delivering measurable operational and commercial results, including 214 percent return on investment for one enterprise self-storage operator, according to Uniti. In addition, 94 percent of its pilots converted into long-term customer contracts, with 306 percent net revenue retention as customers expand across additional properties and workflows. “Commercial real estate runs a trillion dollars of operational labor per year,” said Francesco Decamilli, co-founder and CEO of Uniti. “The way we see it, it’s the same job repeated millions of times, geography by geography, property by property, asset class by asset class. There’s always someone who’s calling about who needs to pay a bill, who needs to file a maintenance request. Property teams work 9 to 5 and customers show up 24/7. For the first time, AI agents are genuinely good enough not to just answer, but to complete workflows end to end, even to transact. They can do the work itself — taking a payment, signing a lease or resolving a maintenance ticket. “So what we’re setting out to build is a unique agentic layer for real estate that works across the entire cycle of the tenant experience.” The Uniti platform integrates with 15 property management systems and uses large language models to locali
bullets: Uniti AI (agentic AI for property management) raised $12M Series A, founded Feb 2024.
Clients include Regus, StorQuest, RHP Properties; runs leasing, maintenance, collections across multifamily, self-storage, senior living.
94% pilot-to-contract conversion; 306% NRR; one self-storage operator achieved 214% ROI.
stories.summary: Uniti, a Manhattan-based agentic AI platform for real estate property managers founded in February 2024, raised a $12M Series A and is experiencing rapid customer adoption across multifamily, self-storage, senior living, and flexible workspace. The platform automates leasing, maintenance, collections, renewals, and reviews via voice, email, SMS, and chat. Customers include Regus and StorQuest, with reported metrics of 94% pilot-to-contract conversion and 306% net revenue retention, plus a 214% ROI for one enterprise self-storage operator.
stories.impact: Uniti's traction in agentic AI for property-management workflows signals the market's readiness to offload labor-intensive back-office and tenant-facing operations to AI. Multifamily operators adopting such platforms early could materially reduce leasing, maintenance, and collections costs, improving asset NOI and pro forma yields—making development feasible in tighter-margin submarkets. However, this is an operational software story, not a demand, supply, capital, or cost signal for development. It may compress operating expense margins industry-wide, lowering exit multiples and asset values over time if not offset by rent growth, but has negligible bearing on the timing, location, or feasibility of new apartment supply in specific markets.
